opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a number we derived from a spreadsheet on day one. It came out of watching how the work actually flows.

What we're building sits at the intersection of AI and formal mathematics, so most of the day-to-day effort is engineering: training infrastructure, data pipelines, the systems that let a model interact with a proof assistant like Lean, evaluation tooling. That's where the bulk of the headcount has to go. But the mathematicians play a different role. They aren't there to produce volume. They're there to set taste: which problems actually matter, what a good formalization looks like, when a model's output is technically valid but mathematically meaningless, and where the frontier really is versus where it just looks hard.

Early on we noticed two failure modes. With too few mathematicians, the engineers would optimize hard toward benchmarks that didn't reflect real mathematical difficulty, and you'd get impressive numbers that didn't mean much. With too many, you'd get wonderful discussions and beautiful problem lists, but not enough people to turn those ideas into systems that scale. Each mathematician ended up acting as a kind of anchor for a cluster of engineers and researchers. Roughly one to fifteen is about where that anchor still feels close to the work, where a mathematician can actually review what their group is producing and push back in real time.

It's also a statement about the kind of mathematician we want. They need to be comfortable working with engineers, reading model outputs, thinking about data. It's a rare profile, so the ratio is partly a reflection of how hard they are to find, too.

And I'd say it's not sacred. As the systems get more capable and start doing more genuinely novel mathematics, I can imagine that ratio shifting, because the bottleneck may move from "can we build it" to "can we judge what it's discovering." At that point you probably need more mathematical judgment in the room, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says the ratio emerged from observing how work flows and describes why roughly 1:15 works; it does not say the number was chosen arbitrarily.

r002.rationale: The response discusses engineering needs and the scarcity of mathematicians, but does not connect the ratio to a funding-imposed headcount limit.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a number we set out to hit. It came out of looking at the work and asking what kind of person actually gets stuck on each piece of it.

When we started Axiom, the obvious thing would have been to hire a lot of mathematicians, because we're building a system that does math. But when you look at where the hard problems are, most of them are engineering problems. Training infrastructure, data pipelines, the formal verification tooling, how you scale search over proofs. Those are things a strong engineer or an ML researcher solves. A mathematician doesn't speed that up, and sometimes they slow it down because they want to understand everything before touching it.

What you really need the mathematician for is taste. Which problems matter, whether a proof the model produced is actually interesting or just technically valid, whether a benchmark is measuring real mathematical ability or just pattern matching on textbook exercises. That's a scarce kind of judgment, but it's also a judgment that one person can spread across a lot of people. One mathematician sitting in a room with fifteen engineers can redirect a lot of effort with a single comment.

So the ratio is more an observation than a policy. We noticed that when a team got much larger than that around a single mathematician, people started making decisions in a mathematical vacuum and wasting cycles. And when the ratio went the other way, the mathematicians were bored, because they were waiting on infrastructure that didn't exist yet. Somewhere around one to fifteen, both sides stayed busy and stayed honest with each other.

I'd also say it reflects something about the stage we're at. Right now the bottleneck is building the machine. As the systems get better, I expect the ratio to shift, because the interesting questions become less about how to train and more about what to ask. But I'd rather adjust that as it happens than design the company around a prediction.

astra-6.text: I’d think of it as a rule of thumb rather than a precise optimum. You want people who can step back, question the assumptions, and think deeply about the mathematical structure of a problem. But you also need a larger team that can turn those ideas into working systems. One in fifteen captures that balance; I wouldn’t claim that fifteen is a magic number.

One in fifteen was a rough way of expressing that balance, rather than a ratio I’d insist every team should follow.
